rows.en: But the early Ḥasidim were not the sect known by the name of Essenes. For the traits and customs that were found among the Essenes are found in their exact opposite among the early Ḥasidim. Among the Essenes it was a rule that moral preparation for perfection is not acquired by sacrifice and burnt offering, but by holiness of deeds and by extreme abstinence (Philo; and see Jost, *History of the Jewish Religion*, p. 104), and they also did not come to the Temple of the Lord to offer sacrifices. But of the early Ḥasidim we are told the opposite: that they would take nazirite vows of their own will in order to bring an offering (Tosefta Nedarim ch. 1), and that they longed to bring an offering (Nedarim 10b⚠1). The early Ḥasidim were neither a sect nor a special association. Rather, just as in all generations the people who went beyond the strict line of the law in keeping the commandments were called by the name "Ḥasidim," so they too were called by this name. But in all that is told of them we have no hint that they were among the noted sages of the Torah in their generation; rather, they were keepers of religion and commandment with great exactness, and their chief merit and excellence lay in deeds, and for this reason they were also recorded under the epithet "men of deed." One saying that is ascribed to the men of deed bears on its face the seal of its time. This saying is the one they used to say at the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing: "Happy is he who has not sinned, and he who has sinned, may he be forgiven." And this saying fits the time after the persecution had ended and the Hasmoneans had defeated the Greeks. For in those days there were many who out of wickedness of heart followed the customs of the Greeks, and these are the "violent among the people" and "those who deal wickedly against the covenant" mentioned in the book of Daniel [Daniel 11:14, 11:32]; but there were also many who could not bear the wrath and fell into the net of temptation from faintness of heart, and turned from the religion against their will, under the compulsion of their oppressors. But when the wrath was over, they returned to God in complete repentance. And now, with regard to those who had stood in their integrity they said: "Happy is he who has not sinned"; and with regard to those who had sinned and returned they said: "and he who has sinned, may he be forgiven." And others said: "Happy is my youth, which has not shamed my old age," and by this they gave thanks to the Lord for having put strength in their hearts to stand in their integrity from beginning to end. But of those who had strayed from the Lord and returned, of them too it was said: "Happy is my old age, which atones for my youth" (Sukkah 53a). However, by the name "the early Elders" are meant the heads of the Torah and the Scribes. Most of the sayings brought in their name speak of matters of impurity and purity, and from their nature it appears that they were very strict in the matter of impurity. We also find that at times the court that came after them either itself retracted and ruled permitted in a matter that had formerly been treated as forbidden, or some of them said to be strict in a certain matter and some of them said to be lenient. And indeed it is surprising when we see that the early Elders disagreed about some matters, since we have an ancient tradition that there was no dispute in Israel except about the laying on of hands alone, and that this dispute remained the only one until, in the days of Hillel and Shammai — the last pair — three more matters were added about which they disagreed. How then shall we say here of the early Elders that they disagreed about several matters? But the matter will be settled if we consider the nature of the subjects about which they disagreed. For in truth the dispute did not come from a difference of understanding in the matter, that one said the law is so and the other said it is not so; rather, they differed in their opinions because of a difference in the degree of piety. And so that the truth may become clear to us, let us give attention to the subject of their dispute itself. Of the early Elders, some used to say half a kav of bones and half a log of blood for all purposes, and some used to say even a quarter-kav and a revi'it of blood for all purposes; and the court after them said a revi'it of blood and a quarter[-kav] of bones for terumah and for holy things, but not for the nazirite and those who perform the Passover offering (Nazir 53a; Tosefta Oholot ch. 4). Now we know that these Elders were among the Ḥasidim, except that beyond their piety they were also among the sages of the Torah whose whole occupation was the expounding of the Torah. And among all the qualities of the human soul there is none whose degrees are so many and so varied as piety. For the quality of piety does not depend on people's opinions and on the judgment of reason; rather, it is for the most part the offspring of excess in the imaginative faculty. And just as excess of the imaginative faculty has many and various degrees, so too has the quality of piety, which is its offspring. Now caution against impurity was the mark of piety in those days. Therefore those whose degree of piety was greater than the degree of piety of their fellows were also stricter about impurity than their fellows. And so we find that the difference in degree was the reason why some of them set a measure for impurity that is smaller than the measure that others set. But we have already seen that most of those who went to excess in the qualities of piety separated from their fellows and went their own way and became a special association, namely the association of the Essenes. And then, after those who went too far had separated from them, it was easy for the rest to come to agreement in their opinions and to go in one way, namely the middle way. Now we understand what is said of the decision of the court after them: they agreed to be strict where there was no harm from another side but there was a fence and a safeguard, namely in terumah and holy things; but they were lenient where the strictness would produce a burden for people, namely in the nazirite and those who perform the Passover offering. And the matter was the same in another halakhah in the laws of impurity: the early Elders were strict to declare the house impure from the sloping eave (katafras) inward (Tosefta Oholot ch. 4, and see Mishnah Oholot 3:3⚠2), and without doubt the opinion of all was not the same about this strictness. But the moderate ones had set aside their own opinion before the opinion of those who went to excess, and they returned to declare it pure after these had separated from them of their own accord and no longer exerted moral pressure on their opinions. Further halakhot were handed down in the name of the early Elders that relied on the midrash of Scripture. The first is what they decreed with regard to keeping away from the impurity of the menstruant. They said: the menstruant ought to be in her separation and kept away from her husband in every way, so that she should not adorn herself, nor paint her eyes, nor rouge her face; and they derived this from the plain sense of the verse that says "and of her that is sick in her impurity" [Leviticus 15:33] (Sifra, end of Metzora; Shabbat 64b). And this extra zeal too is one of the marks of piety. And without doubt the saying "Any woman who makes herself unsightly in the days of her menstruation, the spirit of the sages is pleased with her" (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 2) was founded on this midrash. Another midrash of theirs has survived for us, and it too concerns the laws of impurity (Sifra, Vayikra Dibbura de-Ḥovah ch. 12): "'Or if a soul touch any unclean thing' [Leviticus 5:2] — one might think that even if he touched what touched impurities he would be liable; Scripture says: 'the carcass of an unclean beast, the carcass of unclean cattle, the carcass of unclean creeping things' [Leviticus 5:2] — just as these are distinctive in being fathers of impurity, so anything that is a father of impurity." Now, as for what they said, that one might think that touching anything that touched impurity makes one liable, it may be that those who were excessively strict really thought so, as we have seen that also in the days of Yose ben Yoezer there were those who wanted to be strict in the matter of contact with impurity and wished to go beyond the strict line of the law. If we examine the character of these two midrashim, we still do not find in them a departure from the plain sense of Scripture such as we find among the sages in the later generations. The second midrash is expounded by the rule of general and particular, and it explains the meaning of the general in the likeness of the particular. And we learn from this that neither Hillel, who expounded seven rules, nor R. Ishmael, who expounded thirteen, were the innovators of the midrash of the rules; rather, already long before them their rules were the key with which to expound the Torah. Further, a very precious saying is handed down in the name of the early Elders (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ, Massekhta de-Amalek ch. 2): "Thus the rule goes through all the generations: the rod with which Israel is smitten will in the end itself be smitten. Let every person learn proper conduct from Amalek, who came to destroy Israel, and the Holy One, blessed be He, destroyed him from this world and from the world to come, as it is said: 'for I will utterly blot out' [Exodus 17:14]. And so Pharaoh the wicked, who enslaved Israel — the Holy One, blessed be He, drowned him in the Sea of Reeds, as it is said: 'but He overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Sea of Reeds' [Psalms 136:15]. And so every nation and kingdom that came to harm him, He judged them by the same judgment. Forever they said: with the measure with which a man measures, he is measured, as it is said: 'for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly against them' [Exodus 18:11]. Therefore it is said: 'Write this for a memorial in a book' [Exodus 17:14]." Now this saying as a whole is aimed especially at deeds that were done in those days, and against the efforts of the wicked kingdom to destroy the Jews and to remove the name of Israel from the land. And from the point of view of their ways of expounding the Torah, a new result emerges for us from this saying, namely: the first trace of the rule of extension (ribbui). For when the author of the saying proves that the Holy One, blessed be He, destroyed Amalek in this world and in the world to come from the fact that the blotting out of Amalek is doubled in the Torah, when it says: "for I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek" [Exodus 17:14], this shows us that they expounded the doubling of the word "blot out" to mean that the act of blotting out would continue for a long time, namely in two worlds, in this one and in the one to come; and the reasoning of this midrash is the foundation of the rule of extension. And indeed the sense of doubled forms in the language for this meaning truly lies in the usage of the language, for it is clear that doubling indicates the force of the action; but in the course of time they widened this rule without limit.{v1_06_18:1} And we further learn from their words here that it was their opinion that the narrative part of the Torah was not given to tell the events alone, but that its chief purpose is to teach man knowledge and proper conduct; and they derived this from the saying of the Torah: "Write this for a memorial in a book," meaning that Moses was commanded to write in a book this event that befell them with Amalek, so that it would be a memorial for a later generation, from which it would learn to know the measure of the Holy One, blessed be He. This idea, which emerges for us from this ancient midrash ascribed to the early Elders — that the narrative part of the Torah was not given nor written except to teach man knowledge and proper conduct — is also a source opened for the sages of Israel in the later generations who strive to expound and to search the Torah to the end of its intentions: the masters of the plain sense in their way, the masters of philosophical inquiry in their way, and also the Kabbalists in their way. All of them accepted this idea, that the narratives in the Torah were not written only to tell the events, but that their purpose is more exalted, and they are told for moral and educational benefit; and in the view of the Kabbalists all the narratives of the Torah allude to exalted things and to the secrets of the Torah. But the midrash of the early Elders is the first that founded and explained this view.

1.note: Printed י': (10b); the statement that the early Ḥasidim longed to bring an offering stands in Nedarim 10a. Kept as printed.

2.note: The katafras rule is in Mishnah Oholot 3:7 as far as I know; kept as printed.

rows.en: In those days, when they prevailed over their oppressors who had sought to turn them away from their religion, then too a beginning was made to set up anew the ruined foundations and to restore the religion to its strength. They strove to uphold every Jewish trait, and without doubt various decrees were decreed at that time and ordinances were instituted to make a fence for the Torah. And it is self-evident that they also gave their mind to raising and exalting the Hebrew language. True, its rhetorical power was no longer what it had been in days of old, but its borders widened, so that they were able to speak of every subject; for Aramaic came to its aid, and it also took words from Greek to name various concepts that lacked fitting terms to describe them with Hebrew designations (Graetz, vol. 3, p. 84; *Mishpat Leshon ha-Mishnah*). This widening was of great use to them, for they could use the language in every respect, although the times and the opinions had now changed and new concepts had become known to them. And we have clear traces that the Hebrew language had not died out from among the people. Besides most of the songs that the poets of that time sang about the hardships that befell the nation and about the deliverance by which they were delivered, various other things have been handed down that tell us that they used the Hebrew language: in the popular proverbs that were current in their mouths, in the worship of God in the Temple and outside it, in popular song, in their written notes, and in engraving on a tablet. Such is their saying which was said in the Temple on the day when they circled the altar seven times, and at the time of their departure they said: "Beauty to you, O altar! Beauty to you, O altar!" or "To Yah and to you, O altar; to Yah and to you, O altar."{v1_06_19:1} So too the sayings of the Ḥasidim and the men of deed that were already cited above (Tosefta Sukkah ch. 4, and the Babylonian Talmud there 53a); and what they said at the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing (Sukkah 5:4): "Our fathers who were in this place had their backs toward the Temple and their faces toward the east, and they bowed eastward to the sun; but as for us, our eyes are toward Yah." So too the pleasant phrase that was put in the mouth of the maidens who went out and danced in the vineyards on the Day of Atonement: "Young man, lift up your eyes and see what you choose; do not set your eyes on beauty, set your eyes on family" (end of Ta'anit); and this shows us that the women too used the Hebrew language in their songs. And the same appears from the saying of Bilgah, a priest's daughter⚠1, who apostatized in the days of the war with the Greeks (Tosefta Sukkah ch. 4, and the Babylonian Talmud 56b), who said: "Lykos, lykos [wolf, wolf], how long will you destroy the wealth of Israel, and you do not stand by them in the hour of distress!" So too the inscription that was written on the coins that Simeon the Hasmonean struck was in the Hebrew language and in Hebrew script (Graetz, p. 64). And in documents they used to write: "In the year such-and-such of So-and-so, high priest to God Most High" (Rosh Hashanah 18b). And in the days of the son of Yose ben Yoezer, who consecrated a large sum of his money, they wrote in the book of records that was in the Temple: "Yose ben Yoezer brought in one, and his son brought in six" (Bava Batra 133). And below the tree on which they hung the head and the hand of Nicanor they wrote: "The mouth that spoke in guilt and the hand that stretched out in arrogance" (Yerushalmi Ta'anit 2:12). And in the Hebrew language too they spoke their halakhot and their midrashim that were handed down to us in their names; from their brevity one may judge their origin, and that they were handed down in their very words. Such halakhot, marked by their brevity, are ancient, and many of them are found in the books of the Oral Torah; but because most of them were not handed down in the names of their first authors, we cannot know which of those old halakhot may be ascribed with certainty to that time. But this we can hold with certainty: that many halakhot, as well as new fences and decrees, were born at that time because of the events; and likewise they instituted many things to strike at the crown of their opponents the Sadducees, who at that time began to stand against the teaching of the Pharisees; for then the division of opinions in matters of religion began to come to light more and more.

1.note: So printed; in the Tosefta and the Bavli the woman is Miriam daughter of Bilgah (of the priestly course Bilgah).

rows.en: The Pharisees, the Sadducees, and the Essenes.

Behold, we have seen so far that the time after the victory of the Hasmoneans was fit for widening the matters of religion, and the events compelled it. For this reason the Oral Torah grew and multiplied like a plant. Many ordinances were instituted and many decrees were decreed to make a fence for the Torah, and also many laws and statutes were newly made and learned from the midrash of the verses. And from the account of the events it has become known to us that already in the days of the early Elders the midrash of the Torah began to sprout in such a way that a slight departure from the sense of the words as written could already be seen in it. And all this came from their wish to give a source and a foundation to their traditions and also to their halakhot. The results of this matter, and the results of the events that befell them, were various divisions, by which the members of the nation were divided in their opinions and in several details of belief, until they split into three sects. We see in every religious community that at times some incline away from others in their opinions, for various reasons. There are people who place the glory of every spiritual and scientific statement in the words of the statutes of that religion, and utterly reject reflection and contemplation on the book of statutes of that religion, until they go to the last extreme, not to step even one step beyond the sense of the words as written in the book. And the reason for this is mostly that they see that some light-minded people went astray according to their understanding of the written statutes of the religion, and contemplation became a stumbling block for them, and the departure from the plain sense became a departure from the religion. Over against this we find in every religious community people who go in keeping the religion beyond the bounds of the judgments of their co-religionists, and forbid to themselves what the religion permits, and add stringency upon stringency, until by this they separate themselves from the company of their co-religionists and from their judgments and their customs, and are solitary in their thoughts and in their deeds, and think that by this they will attain nearness to God. And the reason for this always lies in an inclination to superstition and false belief; but what brings about this belief and the inclination to it is mostly the misfortunes of the time. For the hardships and troubles that pass over the heads of men always prepare their hearts to incline after vain beliefs. Such traits, which are in the human soul in general, grew very strong within the Israelite nation. On the one side, the trouble that passed over the head of the holy people like a scourge, "as destruction from the Almighty shall it come" [Isaiah 13:6], worked so that many went to excess in the quality of piety, and despised the pleasures of temporal life, and separated themselves from the community in their deeds, in their customs, and in a piety that passed the bounds. And likewise, on the other side, there were many among the people whose soul did not accept interpretations of the Torah that do not accord with their plain meaning and with the sense of the words as written. Because they saw that many of those who were drawn after the opinions of the Greeks, and interpreted the Torah in agreement with those opinions, went astray in understanding the Torah in its plain sense, they therefore rejected every interpretation that departs from the sense of the words as written, and cast behind their back all interpretations of this kind, and with them also the interpretations of the sages in general, since these too depart from the sense of the words as written. With these opponents sided most of the leading men among the people and the men of wealth. For it is a known thing that the leading men and the men of wealth were never among those who love to widen the borders of enlightenment; and besides this, through the rejection of the interpretations of the sages and of the Oral Torah in general, a benefit grew for them, for they could break the bands of the stringencies, loosen the knots of the decrees, and cast away the cords of the statutes of the Oral Torah; therefore they joined with a willing soul the sages who rose up against the tradition. And these two tendencies quickly became sects, until the people divided into three sects, namely Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes.

footnotes.en: Although according to the reading before us in the Mishnah the latter clause, "even if the king greets him etc.," does not refer back to the first clause but is a separate saying, nevertheless it seems to me that this saying in the latter clause originally came to tell and to teach the character of the Ḥasidim, as I have rendered it in the text; but the author of the Mishnah gave this saying the form of a halakhah, whereas originally and first of all it had the form of a narrative. And in the substance of the matter there is great cause for astonishment here. Certainly it is not surprising of the early Ḥasidim that they would not interrupt even where they were in mortal danger, for indeed that was the character of the Ḥasidim; but it is surprising of the later ones that they fixed it as halakhah, while we see that everywhere they would set aside even the Sabbath for a doubtful danger to life, and for this very reason they opposed the Ḥasidim in the matter of killing snakes and scorpions on the Sabbath. True, Rav Joseph and Rav Sheshet (Berakhot 33a) noticed this, but their words there do not follow the intent of the plain sense of the Mishnah. And from the story of a certain Ḥasid it appears that it was the way of the Ḥasidim not to interrupt under any circumstance, and this is a proof of my words.

R. Ishmael did not expound the doubled forms (Yerushalmi Nedarim 1:1, Sotah 7:5, and in many places), nor did he expound the rule of extension (Shevu'ot 26b and in many places). On the matter of the doubled forms see Tosafot on Sotah (24a), s.v. R. Yonatan, and on Menaḥot (17b), s.v. Mai. This rule of midrash developed in several directions. a) That the doubling indicates that the action is done again at another time besides the present time, without delay between them; and this is the force of the action with respect to its continuance in time. Of this kind is the midrash of the early Elders: maḥoh timḥeh⚠1 — for the world to come. So too hikkaret tikkaret — in the world to come (Sanhedrin 64b; Sifre Shelaḥ 112); pakod tifkod — in the world to come (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ ch. 9⚠2). b) Close to this: ra'oh tir'eh — "you will see what I will do" (Berakhot 31b); ga'oh ga'ah — He is destined to be exalted (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ, Parashat ha-Shirah ch. 2); im bo yavo — a second coming (Sifra Metzora ch. 14); pasoh tifseh — to include the eighth, ninth and tenth [days] (ibid., Tazria ch. 4); amen amen — for the past and for the future (Sotah 18b). c) That the doubling indicates an action which, if it is done, will in the end bring about another like it, whether for reward or for punishment: im shamo'a tishma — if a man has heard, etc., he is made to hear, etc. (Mekhilta Vayassa ch. 1); and im ha'lem ya'limu — etc., in the end, etc. (Sifra Kedoshim ch. 10). d) To indicate an action that is to be done even several times until the purpose is attained: as hokhe'aḥ tokhi'aḥ — even a hundred times (Bava Metzia 31a); ve-rappo yerappe — even four and five times (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 6); abbed te'abbedun — even ten times (Avodah Zarah 45b); shalle'aḥ teshallaḥ — even four and five times (Ḥullin 141a); and im paro'aḥ tifraḥ — even if it returns, etc. (Sifra Tazria ch. 2). e) To indicate that the action is done twice: as im amor yomar — until he says it and repeats it (Kiddushin 22a); im anneh te'anneh — until he afflicts and repeats (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 18). f) Extension to all modes of doing, and of this kind are most of the doubled forms: as hakkeh takkeh — in any case (Sanhedrin 45b); ḥavol taḥbol, hashev tashiv, naton titten, patoaḥ tiftaḥ, ha'anek ta'anik, ha'avet ta'avitennu (see Bava Metzia 31b and in many places); im anneh te'anneh — both much affliction and little affliction (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 18); asham asham (Sifra Vayikra ch. 21); ma'en yema'en — what is the reason⚠3 (Ketubbot 44b). g) To indicate two modes of the action: as akhol ye'akhel — two eatings (Menaḥot 17a); darosh darash — two inquiries (Zevaḥim 101b); shakhav yishkav — two lyings (Sifra Metzora ch. 7). h) To include a thing that is not in the meaning of the verse: as ganov yigganev — to bring in the lost object (Mekhilta ibid. ch. 16); hamer yamir — to include the woman (Temurah 2a); ga'ol yig'alennah — to include the wife and the heir (Sifra Beḥukkotai ch. 4). Thus this rule widened in the course of time without end.

footnotes.en: In these two readings there is nothing but an uncertainty in what was heard, which arose among the hearers because of the likeness of the sounds of the words. For the sound of yofi lekha is quite like the sound of Yah ve-lakh, since the sound of the ḥolam is like the sound of the qamaṣ in pronunciation. And so I conjecture that this too was the reason for the uncertainty there (Sukkah 4:5) about the saying they said at the circling, which according to some was worded "Anna Adonai hoshi'ah na, etc.," and according to R. Judah they said "Ani va-ho hoshi'ah na." For if we consider well and exactly the sound of the words ani va-ho, we find that it is close to the sound of the words anna H' as written; but the small change in it they made because they did not want to pronounce the Name of four letters. But a slight proof emerges for us from this, that in reading the Explicit Name they did not read the yod with a sheva as written, as in our vocalization, but read the yod with a ḥiriq; for then ani va-ho would be close in its pronunciation to anna H' as written. I do not assert this conjecture as settled, but it is closer than the conjecture of the Talmud, which went into gematrias.
